readingInstruction: Read Proverbs 25:1-27:27. A new collection begins, copied by the men of Hezekiah. As you read, notice the images from nature and everyday life, and what the sayings say about friends and enemies.
settingTheScene: Proverbs 25:1 says that these are “also proverbs of Solomon which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied.” They come from the time of Hezekiah, about 700 BC, when the scribes of Judah collected and preserved earlier wisdom. This collection is rich in similes and comparisons, drawn from the world of ordinary experience: snow, rain, apples, thorn bushes, iron.
observation: “It is the glory of God to conceal things, but the glory of kings is to search things out” (25:2).
“A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in a setting of silver” (25:11).
“If your enemy is hungry, give him bread to eat, and if he is thirsty, give him water to drink” (25:21).
“Like a dog that returns to his vomit is a fool who repeats his folly” (26:11).
“Do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you be like him yourself” (26:4), and “Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own eyes” (26:5).
“Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring” (27:1).
“Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy” (27:6).
“Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another” (27:17).
interpretation:
The collection begins with a reflection on knowledge: “It is the glory of God to conceal things, but the glory of kings is to search things out.” God has left much to be discovered. The search for understanding is a kind of honor, and wisdom requires humility before the mystery of God.

The collection is full of word pictures. A word fitly spoken is like gold apples in a silver setting: beautiful, fitting, valuable. A faithful messenger is like cold snow in harvest time. A man without self-control is “like a city broken into and left without walls.” These images ask the reader to slow down and to see the world as a source of wisdom.

Chapter 25’s counsel about enemies is among the most radical in the Old Testament: “If your enemy is hungry, give him bread to eat.” Paul quotes it in Romans 12:20. To give food to an enemy is to overcome evil with good. The “burning coals” are probably a picture of shame leading to repentance.

Chapter 26 gathers the proverbs on fools in a stunning series. The seeming contradiction between 26:4 and 26:5 is intentional. Sometimes a fool should not be answered, so that you do not become like him. Sometimes he should be answered, so that he does not think himself wise. Wisdom is knowing which. Proverbs are not formulas. They require discernment.

Chapter 27 turns to friendship and self-knowledge. “Faithful are the wounds of a friend.” A true friend tells the truth, even when it hurts. “Iron sharpens iron.” We grow through honest relationships. And “as in water face reflects face, so the heart of man reflects the man.” The state of our heart shows in our life. The chapter ends with the call to know the condition of your flocks, a reminder that wealth does not last forever and that careful stewardship matters.
connection: Paul quotes Proverbs 25:21-22 in Romans 12:20 and says, “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.” Jesus said, “Love your enemies” (Matthew 5:44), and showed it on the cross. James 4:13-14 echoes 27:1. Hebrews 10:24 calls believers to “stir up one another to love and good works.” Peter uses 26:11 in 2 Peter 2:22.
application:
Do something kind this week for someone who has been unkind to you.

Ask a trusted friend for honest feedback, and be ready to hear it as a wound that heals.

Think of a “word fitly spoken” that you could offer to someone today.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to make you humble in your search for understanding.
Ask him to teach you to speak a word fitly spoken.
Ask him for the grace to receive the wounds of a friend.
